title: WHAT IF GOD NEVER TOLD YOU THAT?
paragraphs: WHAT IF GOD NEVER TOLD YOU THAT?
“The Heart Is Deceitful” — The dangerous difference between hearing the voice of God and hearing your own desires dressed in spiritual language.
Perhaps one of the most dangerous things a Christian can say is not, “I don't believe in God.”
It is, “God told me.”
Especially when He didn't.
Because once we attach God's name to something we desperately want, we can become almost impossible to correct.

Suddenly, advice becomes opposition. Biblical correction becomes persecution. Accountability becomes a lack of faith. Anyone who questions our decision becomes someone who supposedly doesn't understand what God is doing in our lives.
And without realizing it, we may have stopped following God and started asking God to endorse the life we already wanted.
Read that again.
Have you ever prayed about something while secretly hoping God would give you only one particular answer?
Have you ever wanted a relationship so badly that you interpreted every coincidence as divine confirmation?
Have you ever made a decision out of anger, loneliness, ambition, desperation, or emotional exhaustion, and then convinced yourself that God had placed it on your heart?
Perhaps you weren't intentionally lying.
Perhaps you genuinely believed it.
But sincerity is not the same as spiritual accuracy. A person can sincerely believe something and still be sincerely mistaken.
This is precisely why Scripture gives us a warning that should make every believer examine themselves.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” — Jeremiah 17:9 (KJV)
In the original Hebrew, the passage reads:
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ
ʿĀqōḇ hallēḇ mikkōl, wəʾānuš hûʾ; mî yēḏāʿennû.
A close translation would be:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and incurably sick; who can understand it?”

The Hebrew word עָקֹב (ʿāqōḇ) carries the sense of deceitfulness or crookedness. The word לֵב (lēḇ), translated as “heart,” refers to much more than emotions. In biblical Hebrew, the heart encompasses the inner person, including thoughts, desires, intentions, understanding, and will.
The word אָנֻשׁ (ʾānuš) describes a condition that is desperately sick or incurable.
Jeremiah is exposing something far deeper than emotional instability.
He is exposing humanity's capacity for self-deception.

The heart can manufacture explanations that protect our pride. It can disguise selfishness as self-care, bitterness as discernment, revenge as justice, ambition as calling, lust as love, and disobedience as freedom.
And perhaps most dangerously, it can disguise personal desire as divine direction.

In its immediate context, Jeremiah 17 contrasts the person who places ultimate trust in human strength with the person who trusts in the Lord. The problem is not simply that human beings experience emotions. The problem is misplaced trust and a sinful heart capable of turning away from God.
But notice what God says immediately afterward:
“I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.” — Jeremiah 17:10 (KJV)
God knows what we cannot always recognize within ourselves.
He sees the motive beneath the prayer.
The insecurity beneath the ambition.
The resentment beneath the silence.
The loneliness beneath the attachment.
The pride beneath the spiritual vocabulary.
He knows whether we are genuinely seeking His will or merely seeking His permission.
And that should humble every one of us.
Imagine someone sitting alone at midnight, staring at a message they know they probably shouldn't answer.
They have prayed. They have cried. They have promised themselves they would walk away from a relationship that repeatedly pulls them toward compromise.
But tonight, loneliness feels unbearable.
Then the message arrives.
“I miss you.”
Their heart races.
Suddenly, they remember a sermon about forgiveness. A worship song plays at precisely the right moment. A familiar Bible verse appears on their Facebook feed.
And before long, they whisper:
“Maybe God is telling me to give this another chance.”
But what if those circumstances are not divine instructions?
What if they are interpreting everything through the lens of what they desperately want?

Forgiveness is biblical. Reconciliation can be beautiful. But forgiveness does not automatically require returning to an unsafe relationship, ignoring destructive patterns, or abandoning godly boundaries.
Sometimes, what we call confirmation is simply our desire finding something it can agree with.
Psychology calls a related tendency confirmation bias: our inclination to favor information that supports what we already believe or want to believe.
Scripture has long confronted the spiritual danger of self-deception.
“Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts.” — Proverbs 21:2 (KJV)
We are remarkably skilled at explaining ourselves to ourselves.
That is why a feeling, however powerful, cannot become the final authority over a Christian's life.
You can feel peaceful about something that is wrong.
You can feel uncomfortable about something that is right.
You can feel attracted to something destructive.
You can feel terrified while walking in obedience.
Jesus Himself demonstrated that obedience does not always feel emotionally comfortable.
In Gethsemane, facing the suffering of the cross, He prayed:
“Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42 (KJV)
The original Greek contains these extraordinary words:
πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω.
Plēn mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginesthō.
“Nevertheless, let not my will, but Yours, be done.”
The Greek word θέλημα (thelēma) means will, desire, or intention.
Here we see the sinless Son of God experiencing genuine human anguish without allowing that anguish to turn Him away from perfect obedience to the Father.
Jesus did not pretend the suffering was easy.
He did not deny the weight of what lay before Him.
Yet He surrendered.
And here we encounter one of the most uncomfortable questions of Christian discipleship:
When was the last time you surrendered something you genuinely wanted because you knew it was contrary to God's revealed will?
Not something you had already grown tired of.
Not something that had stopped benefiting you.
Something you still wanted.
Something your emotions were still defending.
Something your flesh was still begging you to keep.
Because following Jesus is not merely inviting Him into our plans. It is surrendering our lives to His lordship.
We live in a culture that constantly tells us to follow our hearts, trust our feelings, protect our happiness, and live our personal truth.
But Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23 (KJV)
The Gospel does not teach us to worship our inner voice.
It teaches us to follow Christ.

That does not mean every desire is sinful, every emotion is unreliable, or every inner impression should be dismissed. God created us with the capacity to feel, love, grieve, rejoice, and desire. Scripture also teaches that God works within His people.
Philippians 2:13 declares that God works in believers both to will and to do according to His good pleasure.
But there is an enormous difference between acknowledging that God can work within our hearts and assuming that everything arising within our hearts comes from God.
The Holy Spirit is God.
Our emotions are not.
Our impressions are not.
Our preferences are not.
And our interpretations are not infallible.
This is why the apostle John wrote:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.” — 1 John 4:1 (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα
Dokimazete ta pneumata.
“Test the spirits.”
The verb δοκιμάζω (dokimazō) means to examine, test, or evaluate something to determine its genuineness.
In context, John is particularly addressing false prophets and the necessity of testing their confession concerning Jesus Christ.
The principle is clear: spiritual claims must not be accepted merely because they sound spiritual.
Likewise, Paul instructs believers in 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21 not to despise prophecies but to test everything and hold firmly to what is good.
Biblical discernment is not unbelief.
It is obedience.
You do not dishonor God by carefully examining whether an impression truly comes from Him. You honor His truth by refusing to casually attach His name to your assumptions.
The Bereans were commended in Acts 17:11 because they examined the Scriptures daily to determine whether the things they were being taught were true.
If even apostolic preaching was examined against Scripture, why should our private feelings be exempt from examination?
No dream, impression, prophecy, coincidence, personal conviction, or emotional experience possesses the authority to overturn what God has revealed in Scripture.
God will not lead you into adultery and call it destiny.
He will not instruct you to deceive someone and call it provision.
He will not authorize bitterness and call it discernment.
He will not encourage spiritual manipulation and call it leadership.
He will not justify exploitation and call it ministry.
He will not contradict His own character to accommodate your desires.
Second Timothy 3:16–17 teaches that Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, correction, reproof, and training in righteousness.
The Greek word θεόπνευστος (theopneustos) means “God-breathed.”
Our feelings must be examined in light of Scripture, not Scripture manipulated to accommodate our feelings.
Yet sometimes we do exactly that.
We search for a verse that agrees with our decision instead of allowing the whole counsel of Scripture to examine our decision.
We collect encouraging passages while avoiding corrective ones.
We listen to sermons that affirm us while rejecting those that confront us.
We surround ourselves with people who tell us what we want to hear and call their agreement confirmation.
And when someone finally challenges us, we say:
“You don't know what God put on my heart.”
But what if the correction you are resisting is something God is using to protect you?
What if the person you have labeled negative is actually demonstrating the courage to love you truthfully?
What if your greatest spiritual breakthrough is not receiving another confirmation, but finally becoming willing to be corrected?
Proverbs 12:15 reminds us that the way of a fool seems right in his own eyes, but a wise person listens to counsel.
Godly counsel is not infallible either. It must also be examined against Scripture. But a heart that refuses every form of correction should be deeply concerned about its own condition.
Pride often becomes most dangerous when it learns to speak Christian.
It knows how to quote verses.
It knows how to pray publicly.
It knows how to say “God's timing,” “my season,” “my calling,” and “the Lord revealed it to me.”
But beneath all that vocabulary, it may still be refusing to surrender.
And perhaps this article is touching something you have been avoiding.
A decision.
A relationship.
A financial pursuit.
A ministry ambition.
A grudge.
A secret compromise.
Something you have repeatedly defended by saying that God placed it on your heart.
You do not have to publicly disclose the details. But you can become honest before the One who already knows them.
Not as an empty religious expression. Not because commenting earns God's favor. Let it be a simple declaration of your willingness to be corrected, healed, and transformed.
David understood the need for this kind of honesty.
After everything he had experienced, including the devastating consequences of his own sin, he knew that human beings needed more than confidence in themselves.
He prayed:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” — Psalm 139:23–24 (KJV)
The Hebrew opening is:
חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
Ḥoqrēnî ʾēl, wəḏaʿ ləḇāḇî.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart.”
David was not asking God to confirm that everything inside him was right.
He was inviting God to expose whatever was wrong.
That is a prayer of spiritual maturity.

“Lord, show me where my desires are deceiving me. Reveal where my wounds are influencing my judgment. Expose where my pride has disguised itself as conviction. And if I am wrong, give me the humility to admit it.”
Imagine how many unnecessary wounds could be avoided if we prayed like that before making life-changing decisions.
Imagine how many relationships, churches, families, and ministries could be protected if we stopped treating personal impressions as unquestionable revelations.
Before declaring, “God put this on my heart,” ask yourself whether the desire agrees with Scripture in its proper context.
Ask whether it reflects the character of Jesus Christ.
Ask whether you are willing to receive correction from mature, trustworthy believers.
Ask whether you would still obey God if His answer disappointed you.
Examine whether your desire is producing the fruit of the Spirit described in Galatians 5:22–23 or feeding the works of the flesh described immediately before it.
And when Scripture does not provide a specific answer about a particular decision, seek wisdom through prayer, sound judgment, godly counsel, and humility.
You do not need to claim a direct revelation for every decision you make.
Sometimes the most spiritually mature thing you can say is:
“I have prayed about this, and I believe this may be the right decision, but I could be mistaken. I am willing for God to correct me.”
There is no shame in acknowledging the limits of your understanding.
The danger is pretending those limits do not exist.
But Jeremiah 17:9 is not the end of the story.
If it were, we would be left with nothing but despair.
The same God who exposes the sickness of the human heart also promises renewal.
In Ezekiel 36:26, speaking of His covenant restoration of Israel, God declares:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.” — Ezekiel 36:26 (KJV)
The Hebrew expression לֵב חָדָשׁ (lēḇ ḥāḏāš) means “a new heart.”
This promise points toward the profound work of divine renewal that Christians understand in light of the new covenant and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
God does not merely expose our brokenness.
He provides redemption.
Jesus did not come simply to teach deceitful hearts how to behave better. He came to save sinners, reconcile us to God, and bring us into new life through His death and resurrection.
At the cross, Christ bore the judgment our sins deserved.
Through His resurrection, He conquered death.
Through faith in Him, we receive forgiveness and are called into a life of repentance, renewal, and obedience.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
Yet spiritual renewal does not mean believers instantly become incapable of error. Christians still need sanctification, correction, discernment, and the ongoing renewal of their minds.
Romans 12:2 tells us to be transformed by the renewing of our minds so that we may discern the will of God.
The Greek word translated as transformed is μεταμορφοῦσθε (metamorphousthe).
It speaks of transformation rather than merely maintaining an outward religious appearance.
The Gospel is not about decorating the old life with Christian vocabulary.
It is about becoming a new person in Christ.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Perhaps you have already made decisions that you claimed were God's will.
Perhaps you used His name to defend something that eventually wounded you or someone else.
Perhaps you manipulated people spiritually without recognizing what you were doing.
Perhaps you are now looking at the consequences of a decision you once celebrated as divine confirmation.
And the shame is overwhelming.
You wonder how you could have been so wrong.
You wonder whether God could ever trust you with anything again.
You wonder whether your failure has permanently disqualified you from a meaningful life of faith.
Hear the Gospel.
Being wrong does not place you beyond the reach of grace. But grace invites you to stop defending what needs to be confessed.
First John 1:9 assures believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
You can repent.
You can acknowledge the truth.
You can seek forgiveness from those you have wounded.
You can accept correction.
You can begin walking in a different direction.

Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence, and restoration does not always mean returning to the position or relationship you once had. But your failures do not have to have the final word over your life.
Jesus Christ is greater than the worst chapter of your story.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create a community of people who pretend to have perfect hearts, but to point imperfect people toward a perfect Savior.
Not to manufacture emotional experiences, but to encourage genuine biblical discipleship.
Not to build faith around personalities, but to continually bring people back to the authority of Scripture and the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
There may come a day when your emotions are louder than your discernment, and you will need to remember these truths.
Your simple act of sharing could place biblical encouragement in front of someone who is wrestling with a decision they have not told anyone about.

Scripture recognizes the importance of supporting those who labor in Gospel ministry. Galatians 6:6 encourages those receiving instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach them, while 1 Corinthians 9:14 affirms the legitimacy of material support for Gospel workers.
If you desire to glorify God through your financial stewardship, supporting faithful Gospel-centered work can be one meaningful expression of that desire.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us, God loves a cheerful giver, not someone giving under compulsion.
Salvation is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
And before you leave, wherever you are right now, consider making this your prayer:
“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I confused my desires with Your direction. Forgive me for using Your name to defend my pride, my fears, my ambitions, and my disobedience.
Search the places within me that I have been afraid to examine. Correct what needs correction. Heal what needs healing. Remove what keeps drawing me away from You.
Give me a heart that loves truth more than affirmation, obedience more than comfort, and Your presence more than the fulfillment of my personal desires.
Teach me to examine everything in the light of Your Word. Give me wisdom through Your Holy Spirit, humility to receive correction, and courage to repent when I am wrong.
Even when Your will is different from mine, help me trust Your goodness.
Let my life belong to You.
Not my will, Lord, but Yours be done.
In Jesus' name, Amen.”
Never forget that the goal of Christianity is not to become so confident in your own heart that you never question it.
It is to become so devoted to Jesus Christ that you are willing to let Him transform it.
The next time you feel something powerful rising within you, resist the temptation to immediately declare, “God told me.”
Pray.
Examine Scripture.
Seek wisdom.
Remain teachable.
And remember that the God who loves you enough to comfort you also loves you enough to correct you.
Sometimes His mercy looks like a closed door.
Sometimes His wisdom reaches you through an uncomfortable conversation.
Sometimes His grace exposes the very thing you have spent years protecting.
And sometimes the greatest evidence of spiritual growth is not that you finally received what your heart wanted, but that you became willing to surrender it to Christ.
The heart may write a beautiful story to justify its rebellion, but only Jesus can rewrite that story into redemption.
